newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks, bonds off sharply on flurry of rumors.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks, bonds off sharply on flurry of rumors.

text.p: U.S. stocks and bonds fell sharply Wednesday on a flurry of unsubstantiated rumors and increasing speculation that Japan was no longer willing to be a big buyer of U.S. Treasury bonds.
International Business Machines Corp declined comment on a rumor that it was about to issue a profit warning. A source said he doubted the IBM rumor.
Goldman, Sachs & Co, addressing another rumor, said its market strategist Abby Joseph Cohen, long bullish on U.S. stocks, had not made any new comments.
One trader said he thought the selloff amid and overheating market was healthy. He said he expected the market would stabilize quickly.

By 1030 EST/1530 GMT the Dow industrials were off 60 to 6413. The Dow had been off close to 100 points in the first 15 minutes of trading, triggering New York Stock Exchange curbs on program trading as it fell 50 points.

"The tone is very nervous because we've had a huge runup in such a short period of time," said another trader. The trader also said big institutional investors had stepped to the sidelines and there did not seem to be any general panic.
The 30-year U.S. Treasury issue was off nearly a point at 1035 EST/1535 GMT, pushing the yield up to 6.55 percent.

Traders said a new focus in the bond market was whether Japan would continue to support the U.S. Treasury market. John Breazeale, president of Weiss Money Management Inc in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla., said the heavy ownership of U.S. debt by foreigners has been an "obvious problem" for some time. He noted that foreigners own almost $1 trillion out of a total of $5.1 trillion outstanding.
He said there is always the possibility Japan could stop its purchases or even sell some of its holdings.

Breazeale said if foreigners shunned U.S. debt, then due to supply and demand factors, interest rates would rise even without any pickup in inflation. "We have felt for a long time that the precipitant (of falling bond prices) will be foreign owners of U.S. debt scared by something, we dont know what yet. It could be inflation, something political, or social -- nobody knows."
Bond traders said foreigners, mainly large Japanese corporations, were heavy sellers of U.S. Treasuries during the Tokyo and early London sessions.

"Everybody knows that foreign investors have been buying huge amounts of U.S. assets," said James Glassman, economist and vice president at Chase Securities Inc. "People see these large flows and they justifiably believe these capital flows are holding interest rates down globally. But we are nervous because we wonder how sustainable this is."

But Glassman said there are other parts to the picture. He said as long as the U.S. economy is marked by low, stable inflation and healthy growth, U.S. assets will remain attractive and foreigners will buy them.

Markets have been nervous since late last week, when Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan warned about "irrational exuberance" in the markets. A decline in markets all over the world on Friday was attributed to Greenspan's comments. U.S. stocks recovered part of their early losses Friday and the Dow industrials rose Monday and again Tuesday.
But some traders were still wondering if Greenspan's next move to deflate the markets would be an interest rate hike.
The dollar started lower in New York Wednesday but then stabilized. It was trading at 1.5392/99 marks and 112.85/95 yen at 1115 EST/1615 GMT.

Meanwhile, a variety of rumors beset the markets. Among them: IBM was rumored about to issue an earnings warning; long -time bull Abby Joseph Cohen of Goldman Sachs was said to have turned bearish; the U.S. might bomb Iran in January; a major Japanese bank might fold due to derivative losses; Japanese investors were said to be shedding U.S. bond holdings.

"The stock market was vulnerable at this level. We'll see more (rumors). The market just doesn't go straight up," said Ken Ducey, director of trading at BT Brokerage, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Bankers Trust.
The long bond shed 1-23/32 to yield 6.62 percent.
It was the highest yield since November 6's close.
"My feeling is we're getting the great margin call of all time on bonds," said Michael Metz, Oppenheimer and Co's chief investment strategist.

Wall Street was greeted by tame wholesale inflation data this morning. November producer prices rose 0.4 percent as energy prices posted the biggest jump since April. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the core rose 0.1 percent.
The Street faces November consumer prices and retail prices on Thursday.
Losers outpaced gainers 21-5 on very heavy NYSe volume of about 490 million shares.

The Dow just on Friday fell about 145 points before ending off 56 points. Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan's cautionary comments on "irrational exuberance" in financial markets late Thursday triggered global selling.
Among individual stocks, IBM fell 1-7/8 to 156-1/8. The company declined comment on the market speculation and said it planned no press releases today.
Micron rose two to 36 after it said its balance sheet at the end of the first quarter was better than expected.
A Micron executive also told the Montgomery Securities conference that it expects first-quarter revenues to be flat to slightly above fourth-quarter revenues.
Philip Morris continued to rise, up two to 118-7/8. Sanford Bernstein reiterated its outperform rating.
MoneyGram Payment Systems Inc, a non-bank provider of consumer money wire transfer services, surged 1-5/8 to 13-5/8 in its first day of trading.
Another IPO, Skymall Inc, an in-flight catalog company that sells merchandise to airline passengers, rose 3/4 to 8-3/4.
